summary:
Caquetá is a department of Colombia and stands under the national framework of Colombia. The department-specific signal in the source inventory concerns organised violence rather than statute: The Guardian reported on 30 July 2024 that armed groups in Caquetá were running a 'social cleansing' campaign, distributing flyers on the street and via WhatsApp that named 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets.

The campaign has produced forced displacement of trans residents. A trans woman and local election candidate was told by three armed men that she had one week to leave town; she hid for a week and then fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend had been killed. The same reporting states that discrimination in Caquetá limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, narrowing the economic options that would otherwise let a resident or visitor remain independent of exposure.

Nationally the same reporting counted 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024, figures that give the Caquetá flyer campaign its wider context. A separate case, the killing of Sara Millerey in Bello, Antioquia on 4 April 2025, was filmed and circulated as a viral video on 5 April; she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon, and despite police questioning of local residents and an urgent investigation ordered by the president, no one was arrested. Thirteen trans people were killed by hate in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025. Both incidents fall outside Caquetá and are carried here only as evidence of the national pattern of lethal anti-trans violence a visitor to the department faces.
tangentialFactors:
The threat model in Caquetá is driven by armed groups operating outside the state rather than by routine policing, which distinguishes it from departments where exposure runs through official channels. Flyers circulated both physically and on WhatsApp, so the kill-list messaging reaches residents who never encounter the armed groups directly.

Displacement is the practical outcome documented for trans women who are named or identified: one candidate fled at night after a one-week deadline, and the reporting describes trans women in the department as having few economic options beyond hairdressing and sex work, which constrains where a person can relocate to.
localsOnly:
Trans women in Caquetá face a documented narrowing of lawful employment to hairdressing or sex work, according to The Guardian's 30 July 2024 reporting. Sex work in turn increases exposure to the armed groups running the 'social cleansing' campaign, since the flyers name prostitutes among their declared targets.

A trans woman standing as a local election candidate was served an eviction deadline by three armed men, indicating that political visibility by trans residents is treated as a targeting trigger in the department. A second trans woman reported that a friend had been killed, though the source does not name the victim or give a date.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not identify the armed groups responsible for the Caquetá flyer campaign, nor give the number of flyers distributed, the towns affected, or any arrests connected to the campaign. Whether any Caquetá-specific protection order, relocation programme, or prosecutor unit has been activated for the named trans residents is not sourced here.

The count of 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024 is a national figure with no departmental breakdown, so Caquetá's share of those killings is unresolved. The identity and outcome of the friend reported killed by the second trans woman are likewise not sourced.
